prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and its experimental realization in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B009, to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. The Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall prediction gave a classification of insulators by band topology, with protected edge states that were then observed in HgTe quantum wells. That is a discovery in nature with a clear theoretical origin, a decisive experiment, and about two decades of independent confirmation by transport, ARPES and STM. I tested it against the round-1 exchange on its scientific merits and not on the count of supporters. The one change I make is to the citation. After Eriksson's and Johansson's comments I now name the HgTe realization explicitly, so that the text states what the three names actually delivered, the two-dimensional step, and does not read as a claim over the whole topological-insulator field. This also answers the chair's question on distinctness from 2016: that prize recognised topological phase transitions and topological phases in model systems, whereas this one recognises band topology of real, time-reversal-invariant insulators, a predicted invariant and a material in which it was seen.
statement.case_against: The credit is not clean and the three-name limit cannot make it so. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang identified HgTe as the material, and Hasan's group provided the first three-dimensional observations, so a narrow citation leaves out serious claimants and must say plainly that it does so. The 2016 prize also leaves some members seeing a second helping on a topological theme, and technological payoff is still limited. Against B026, I accept that Katori and Ye have the cleaner attribution boundary, and I cannot verify magic-wavelength priority or the claims of other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups from the materials supplied.

responses.point: Eriksson separates the 2D quantum spin Hall step from the 3D observation by Hasan, wants a narrow citation, and says Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal should be left out openly rather than papered over.
responses.response: In round 1 I was inclined to treat the 3D step as a possibly larger prize. His position is the more honest one: the committee should decide once that the 2D prediction and realization is the discovery being honoured, and then word the citation so that it does not reach into three dimensions. I have adopted that. Where I still differ is that I do not regard Hasan as merely a space casualty either. If the committee wanted the 3D framing, the right course would be to change the configuration around a different centre, not to bolt Hasan on in place of Mele, whose Z2 invariant underlies both steps.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B026 for its clean two-name credit and mature, independently reproduced physics, but sees the overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes as the main risk and calls the choice with B009 a close call.
responses.response: I take the attribution contrast with B026 seriously and keep it as my first alternative. But the overlap objection that he raises against lattice clocks weighs on it more than the 2016 objection weighs on B009. Lattice clocks refine a precision-metrology programme that the 2005 and 2012 prizes already honoured, and the magic-wavelength priority cannot be checked in what we have. B009 introduced a new organising principle, and its credit problem is a matter of who is omitted, not of whether the discovery is separable. His concession that B009 is acceptable if B026 does not carry suggests we differ in weighting, not in the facts, and I do not think an unverifiable priority claim should outweigh a conceptually new, thoroughly confirmed result.

responses.point: Johansson agrees that Hasan versus Mele is the hardest part of B009, asks that the 2D versus 3D decision be made once and well, and says a different candidate might be cleaner if no defensible split exists.
responses.response: I think the split is defensible. The Fu-Kane-Mele extension and Hasan's observation in Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 build on the Z2 framework that Kane and Mele introduced, which is why Mele stays and why a citation limited to the quantum spin Hall state and its HgTe realization is coherent without Hasan. I accept her demand that the argument be explicit, and my citation wording is meant to carry it. I also respect that she has put B010 aside on timing and her own position; I agree that the 2025 circuit prize makes it a poor choice this year.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube (B024) to B009 and, as chair, asks whether the 2016 prize is disqualifying and whether the omission of Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Hasan has been acknowledged.
responses.response: I accept the chair's question on the 2016 prize and answer that it is not disqualifying, for the reason in my case for. On B024, nothing in the exchange has supplied a partner for Halzen, so I still cannot support a single name for a result of that scale; I treat the neutrino window as a prize for a later year once the credit can be defended.

uncertainties: Whether the committee settles that the 2D quantum spin Hall step is the discovery honoured and that Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposers are acknowledged as omitted, rather than implied to be covered.

How a reader will weigh the 2016 prize on topological phases against this prize; my distinction between model topological phases and band topology of real insulators is a judgement, not a settled fact.
My historical attributions, including Fu-Kane-Mele and magic-wavelength priority, rest on recollection and have not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: my PhD supervisor David Gross, mentor Hector Rubinstein and co-author Thomas Van Riet are not among the credited names for any shortlisted candidate. This is unchanged from round 1. I note the disclosures of Johansson (B010), Kroll (B026), Lindroth, Eriksson and Pearce as made in the chair's summary.
